title: Edge VPC Gateway integration lab notes
summary: Working lab notes and compatibility matrix for integrating a customer VPC with Redwood Edge Gateway. Focus: segmentation, Terraform module quirks, upgrade/rollback options, and a small runbook for staging validation.
content:
Purpose:
- Capture the hands-on experiments we ran to integrate customer VPCs with the Edge Gateway appliance (virtual/physical) and the set of Terraform snippets and module behaviors that tripped us.
- Produce a concise staging runbook engineers can run during Customer Onboarding/Upgrade rehearsals.

Scope:
- This is focused on L3-L4 network, route tables, egress controls, and the infra-as-code surface (TF modules + small wrapper scripts).
- Not covering full HSM/KMS integration or RBAC post-install; those are separate playbooks.

Lab goals (what we validated):
1) Establishing an encrypted peering/tunnel from a customer-managed VPC to the Edge Gateway in a dedicated subnet and verifying prefix routing + path MTU.
2) Confirming segmentation rules can be applied selectively per-tenant using security group equivalents on the gateway.
3) Exercising a schema for canary upgrades of gateway firmware/software while preserving active connections.
4) Validating Terraform idempotence across a typical customer change (add CIDR, rotate shared secret).

Topology sketch (ASCII):
- Customer-VPC (10.12.0.0/16) ---[VPN/IPSec or FC]--> Edge-GW-subnet (rgw-edge-az-a) ---[internal routable]--> Redwood Private Plane
- Important: Edge GW runs two NICs: public (control/bg) and private (data/kv-cache).

Key findings from experiments:
- Terraform module v1.3.0 (vpc-edge-gateway) implicitly assumes provider aliasing for "edge" vs "controlplane". If aliases are missing TF will recreate resources during a provider change. Workaround: pin provider aliases in the wrapper module and add a provider version constraint in the root module.
- Route propagation: some customer accounts (esp. older on-prem SDWAN stacks) dropped /30 routes causing asymmetric paths; we found adding explicit static route entries in the edge-gateway config (via the config API) fixed egress pathing for services that do health checks from outside.
- MTU: when transit uses GRE-over-IPsec the effective MTU can drop to ~1380; our runtime failed with large batched websocket frames. Short-term fix: enable MSS clamping on the gateway. Longer-term: health-check tooling should reduce batch sizes for on-prem customers with legacy SDWAN.
- Canary upgrade: we could maintain existing sessions if the gateway supports warm-restart of the L2/L3 forwarding plane. The upgrade procedure must first drain new session allocations (iptables|conntrack rules) then switch the control plane; otherwise TCP sessions drop.

Terraform snippets and notes (practical):
- Example provider pinning (wrapper root):
  - alias "edge_cp" -> provider "aws" region = var.edge_region
  - alias "ctrl_cp" -> provider "aws" region = var.control_region
- Important var knobs to expose to customers:
  - customer_allowed_cidrs (list) -- default [] but validate /16 min length to avoid very large supernets that expand route tables.
  - tunnel_mtu_override (number) -- null allows auto-negotiation; explicit set required for legacy SDWAN.
  - should_create_eip (bool) -- some customers require static public IPs for firewall rules.
- Known TF pitfalls:
  - aws_vpc_peering with overlapping cidrs silently errors on plan vs apply; do an explicit cidr_overlap precheck in a wrapper script (small python/.tfdata check).
  - aws_route_table_propagation vs aws_vpn_connection routes ordering causes plan diff noise; keep a single route table per-edge-gateway to reduce churn.

Onboarding staging runbook (minimal checklist):
1) Pre-checks (customer pre-call): collect ASN, CIDR(s), preferred egress IPs, firewall ACL templates, and whether SDWAN is NATing.
2) Terraform dry-run: run terraform plan with provider aliases set to a staging AWS account. Inspect outputs: cloud-route-ids and eip allocations.
3) Provision Edge GW in a staging VPC with the exact CIDR layout the customer will use (mimic MTU and NAT behaviors).
4) Establish tunnel and run 30-minute soak with proxy load (simulate bursts + KV cache warmups). Monitor: RTT, packet-loss, conntrack count.
5) Canary upgrade rehearsal: apply upgrade to 10% of sessions (we simulated by shifting a service tag), observe session persistence.
6) Rollback test: force a rollback and ensure routes, secrets, and IP allocations come back to expected state w/o leaking ephemeral keys.

Upgrade strategy (safe path):
- Blue/Green for control plane, Warm-Restart for data plane. Sequence:
  a) Create new control plane instances on new subnet/ASG with config drift minimized.
  b) Drain new session allocations on old instances (stop accepting new tunnels).
  c) Switch BGP peerings gradually (if used) to new control plane.
  d) Validate connectivity for key endpoints (health endpoints + sample calls).
  e) Decommission old control plane after 24h confirmation.

Rollback checklist:
- Keep previous TF state snapshot in S3 with timestamped key.
- Snapshot existing edge-gateway configs via API before upgrade.
- Have a script that re-applies previous config and triggers conntrack flush in a controlled window.
- Communicate to customer a 10-minute estimated outage window if rollback is needed.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide policy for allowed customer CIDR sizes; large /12s blow up route table in some partner clouds. (action: policy doc to product team)
- Add automated preflight that validates SDWAN vendor behaviors (NAT, MSS, fragmentation). (action: small probe-runner PoC)
- Can we expose a telemetry hook so customers can share on-prem network telemetry to our staging runner securely? Legal/TLS concerns.

Quick reference commands (for lab):
- terraform init -backend-config=staging.tfbackend
- terraform plan -var-file=staging.tfvars -out=staging.plan
- tfstate snapshot: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-tfstate/edge/vpc-prod.tfstate ./snap-2026-02-20.tfstate
- api config dump: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $EDGE_API_TOKEN" https://edge-staging.redwood.internal/api/v1/config > edge-config.json

Appendix: small troubleshooting checklist when tunnels fail:
- verify pre-shared key match (PSK) and IKE times (phase1/phase2)
- check BGP session counters and that ASNs don't collide
- confirm route table has the specific /32 or /30 routes not aggregated away
- confirm MSS clamp is applied if large websocket frames are failing

Notes-to-self / informal:
- We should add a tiny terraform validation module that runs local checks and emits a clear non-zero exit code if overlapping CIDRs or missing provider aliasing found. Saves 30m debugging on calls.
- Today Miguel and Tom saw one weird case where a Palo Alto next-hop rewrite caused health checks to come from a different IP; need to document vendor-specific caveats.

If you run this lab, drop follow-up findings in the comments below and add a mini-matrix entry: vendor, MTU observed, conntrack peak, lesson learned.
